'''Keybase''' is a [[Key server (cryptographic)|key directory]] that maps [[social media]] identities to encryption keys (including, but not limited to [[Pretty Good Privacy|PGP]] keys) in a publicly auditable manner.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/sigchain|title=Sigchain {{!}} Keybase Docs|website=keybase.io|access-date=2019-06-09}}</ref> Additionally it offers an [[End-to-end encryption|end-to-end encrypted]] chat and [[cloud storage]] system,<ref name="KE">{{Cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/2017/02/09/keybase-encrypted-chat/|title=Keybase's encrypted chat works with accounts you already have|last=Dalton|first=Andrew|date=2017-09-02|website=Engadget|access-date=2017-06-05}}</ref><ref name="KI">{{Cite news|url=https://techcrunch.com/2016/02/05/keybase-introduces-end-to-end-encrypted-file-sharing-service/|title=Keybase Introduces End-To-End Encrypted File Sharing Service|last=Russell|first=Jon|date=2016-05-02|work=TechCrunch|access-date=2017-05-06}}</ref> called Keybase Chat and the Keybase Filesystem respectively. Files placed in the public portion of the filesystem are served from a public endpoint,<ref name="KW" /> as well as locally from a filesystem [[Union mount|union-mounted]] by the Keybase client.<ref name="UK">{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/kbfs/understanding_kbfs|title=Understanding the Keybase filesystem|website=Keybase|access-date=2017-09-26}}</ref>

Keybase supports publicly connecting [[Twitter]], [[GitHub]], [[Reddit]], and [[Hacker News]] identities, including websites and domains under one's control, to encryption keys. It also supports [[Bitcoin]], [[Zcash]], [[Stellar (payment network)|Stellar]], and QRL wallet addresses.<ref name="KW">{{cite web|url=https://www.fastcompany.com/3044306/keybase-wants-to-make-serious-encryption-accessible-to-mere-mortals|title=Keybase Wants To Make Serious Encryption Accessible To Mere Mortals|website=Fast Company|last1=Fleishman|first1=Glenn|date=7 May 2015 |access-date=5 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="KE" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/blog/keybase-and-zcash|title=Keybase chooses Zcash|website=The Keybase Blog|access-date=2018-02-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://keybase.io/blog/keybase-stellar-launch|website=The Keybase Blog|title=Stellar wallets for all Keybase users|access-date=2019-09-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/blog/keybase-proofs-for-mastodon-and-everyone|title=Keybase 's Mastodon, and how to get your site on Keybase|website=keybase.io|access-date=2019-06-08}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-04-24|title=QRL and Keybase|url=https://www.theqrl.org/blog/qrl-and-keybase/|access-date=2021-04-06|website=www.theqrl.org|language=en}}</ref> Keybase has supported [[Coinbase]] identities since initial public release, but ceased to do so on March 17, 2017, when Coinbase terminated public payment pages.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://keybase.io/blog/abrupt-termination-of-coinbase-support|title=Abrupt Termination of Coinbase Support|website=The Keybase Blog|publisher=Keybase, Inc|access-date=5 June 2017}}</ref> In general, Keybase allows any service with public identities to integrate with Keybase.<ref name="KW" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/proof_integration_guide|title=Proof Integration Guide {{!}} Keybase Docs|website=keybase.io|access-date=2019-06-08|archive-date=2019-06-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190608212519/https://keybase.io/docs/proof_integration_guide|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On May 7, 2020, Keybase announced it had been acquired by [[Zoom Video Communications|Zoom]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Keybase joins Zoom|url=https://keybase.io/blog/keybase-joins-zoom|website=keybase.io|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref> as part of Zoom's "plan to further strengthen the security of [its] video communications platform".<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Zoom Acquires Keybase and Announces Goal of Developing the Most Broadly Used Enterprise End-to-End Encryption Offering|url=https://blog.zoom.us/wordpress/2020/05/07/zoom-acquires-keybase-and-announces-goal-of-developing-the-most-broadly-used-enterprise-end-to-end-encryption-offering/|date=2020-05-07|website=Zoom Blog|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref> Since the acquisition, development has stopped, but the service has been kept functional.

== Identity proofs ==
Keybase allows users to ''prove'' a link between certain online identities (such as a [[Twitter]] or [[Reddit]] account) and their encryption keys. Instead of using a system such as [[OAuth]], identities are proven by posting a signed statement as the account a user wishes to prove ownership of. This makes identity proofs publicly verifiable – instead of having to trust that the service is being truthful, a user can find and check the relevant proof statements themselves, and the Keybase client does this automatically.

== App ==
In addition to the web interface, Keybase offers a client application for [[Windows]],<ref name="KO">{{Cite news|url=http://www.macworld.com/article/3168585/encryption/keybase-offers-encrypted-chat-where-you-control-all-the-pieces.html|title=Keybase offers encrypted chat where you control all the pieces|last=Fleishman|first=Glenn|date=Feb 15, 2017|work=Macworld|access-date=June 8, 2017}}</ref><ref name="KA">{{Cite news|url=https://nakedsecurity.sophos.com/2017/05/31/keybase-adds-end-to-end-encryption-to-messages-on-the-web/|title=Keybase adds end-to-end encryption to messages on the web|last=Dunn|first=John E|date=May 31, 2017|work=Naked Security|access-date=June 8, 2017|archive-date=27 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200327012517/https://nakedsecurity.sophos.com/2017/05/31/keybase-adds-end-to-end-encryption-to-messages-on-the-web/|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Mac OS|Mac]],<ref name="KO" /><ref name="KA" /> [[Android (operating system)|Android]],<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://androidcommunity.com/keybase-encrypted-chat-now-available-on-android-20170512/|title=Keybase encrypted chat now available on Android|last=Hoff|first=John|date=May 12, 2017|work=androidcommunity.com|access-date=June 8, 2017}}</ref><ref name="KA" /> [[iOS]],<ref name="KA" /> and most desktop [[Linux distribution]]s,<ref name="KA" /> written in [[Go (programming language)|Go]] with an [[Electron (software framework)|Electron]] front end. The app offers additional features to the website, such as the end-to-end encrypted chat, teams feature, and the ability to add files to and access private files in their personal and team Keybase Filesystem storage. Each device running the client app is authorized by a [[Signature (cryptography)|signature]] made either by another device or the user's [[Pretty Good Privacy|PGP]] key. Each device also has a device-specific key to enable the user to establish their identity using any of their devices.<ref>{{cite web |last=Keybase Team |title=Keybase's New Key Model: device-specific NaCl keys |url=https://keybase.io/blog/keybase-new-key-model |website=Keybase Blog |date=25 September 2015 |access-date=2 December 2025}}</ref>

== Chat ==
Keybase Chat is an end-to-end encrypted chat built in to Keybase launched in February 2017. A distinguishing feature of Keybase Chat is that it allows Keybase users to send messages to someone using their online aliases (for example a [[reddit]] account), even if they haven't signed up to Keybase yet.<ref name="KE" />

If the recipient (the online alias owner) has an account on Keybase, they will seamlessly receive the message. If the recipient doesn't have a Keybase account, and later signs up and proves the link between the online account and their devices, the sender's device will [[Rekeying (cryptography)|rekey]] the message for the recipient based on the public proof they posted, allowing them to read the message. Since the Keybase app checks the proof, it avoids [[trust on first use]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/blog/keybase-chat|title=Introducing Keybase Chat|website=The Keybase Blog|publisher=Keybase, Inc|access-date=February 12, 2018}}</ref>

== Keybase Filesystem (KBFS) ==

-->
[[File:Meekwire_Keybase_-_James_Gordon_Meek.png|thumb|Keybase screenshot showing a user's keys]]
Keybase allows users to store up to 250 GB<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/images/blog/teams/teams-splash-announcement.png|title=FYI - we changed the default KBFS plan to 250GB instead of just 10GB. Very few people are hitting the limit so it's less work to let them go past it than deal with UX around upgrading right now.|website=Keybase (via Wayback Machine)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171222221055/https://keybase.io/images/blog/teams/teams-splash-announcement.png|access-date=June 11, 2018|archive-date=2017-12-22}}</ref> of files in a cloud storage called the Keybase Filesystem for free. There are no storage upgrades available, but paid plans allowing for more data are planned.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/kbfs|title=Keybase|website=keybase.io|access-date=2019-02-10}}</ref> The filesystem is divided into three parts: public files, private files, and team files. On [[Unix-like]] machines, the filesystem is [[Mount (computing)|mounted]] to <code>/keybase</code>, and on [[Microsoft Windows]] systems it is usually mounted to the K drive.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/kbfs|title=Introducing the Keybase filesystem|website=Keybase|access-date=2017-09-26}}</ref> Currently, mobile versions of the Keybase client can only download files from kbfs, and can not mount it. However, they do support operations such as rekeying files as necessary. In October 2017 Keybase brought out end-to-end encrypted [[Git]] repositories.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/blog/encrypted-git-for-everyone|title=Keybase launches encrypted git|website=The Keybase Blog|publisher=Keybase, Inc|access-date=June 11, 2018}}</ref>

=== Public files ===
Public files are stored in <code>/public/''username''</code>, and are publicly visible. All files in the public filesystem are automatically [[Digital signature|signed]] by the client.<ref name="UK" /> Only the user who the folder is named after can edit its contents, however, a folder may be named after a comma-separated list of users (e.g. a folder <code>/public/''foo,bar,three''</code> would be editable by the users ''foo'', ''bar'', and ''three'').<ref name="UK" />

Public files can be accessed by any user. Single user folders are displayed at {{URL|https://keybase.pub/}} and are also accessible by opening the directory in the mounted version of the filesystem. Multi user folders (such as <code>/public/''foo,bar,three''</code>) are only accessible through the mounted version of the system.

=== Private files ===
Private files are stored in <code>/private/''username''</code>, and are only visible to ''username''. Private folders, like public folders, can be named after more than one user (e.g. a folder <code>/private/''foo,bar,three''</code> would be readable and editable by the users ''foo'', ''bar'', and ''three''). Private files can also be read only for users after "#" (e.g. a folder <code>/private/''writer1,writer2,#reader1,reader2''</code> would be readable and editable by the users ''writer1'' and  ''writer2'' but only readable for ''reader1'' and ''reader2'').<ref name="UK" />  Unlike public files, all private files are both encrypted and signed before being uploaded, making them end-to-end encrypted.<ref name="KI" />

=== Team files ===
Team files are stored in <code>/team/''teamname''</code>, and are publicly visible to team members. All files in the team filesystem are automatically [[Digital signature|encrypted and signed]] by the client.<ref name="UK" /> Only users who are marked as writers can edit its contents, however, any readers can access the files stored there.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/kbfs/understanding_kbfs|title=KBFS - Understanding KBFS {{!}} Keybase Docs|website=keybase.io|access-date=2019-06-09}}</ref>

== Teams ==
In September 2017, Keybase launched Keybase Teams.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://fortune.com/2017/09/18/slack-okcupid-sparknotes-encryption-keybase-chat-app/|title=First They Made OkCupid and SparkNotes. Now They're Taking on Slack|last=Hackett|first=Robert|date=18 September 2017|work=Fortune Tech|access-date=21 September 2017}}</ref> A team is described as "...a ''named'' group of people."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/command_line/teams_alpha|title=Teams for Keybase|website=Keybase.io|access-date=September 21, 2017|archive-date=October 27, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181027143249/https://keybase.io/docs/command_line/teams_alpha|url-status=dead}}</ref> Each team has a private folder in the Keybase filesystem, and a number of chat channels (similar to [[Slack (software)|Slack]]). Teams can also be divided into "subteams" by placing a [[Full stop|<code>.</code>]] in the team name. For example, <code>wikipedia.projects</code> would be a subteam of <code>wikipedia</code>, while <code>wikipedia.projects.foobar</code> would be a subteam of <code>wikipedia.projects</code> (and therefore, also of <code>wikipedia</code>).

=== Team administration ===
<!-- I would _greatly_ appreciate help on this section - https://keybase.io/docs/teams/index has docs -->
Teams are largely administered by adding signatures to a chain. Each signature can add, remove, or change the membership of a user in a team, as well as when changes are made to subteams.

Each chain starts with a signature made by the team owner, with subsequent actions signed on by team admins or users.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://keybase.io/docs/teams/details|title=Teams: Naming, Merkle Tree Integration, And Signature Chains|website=Keybase|access-date=2017-09-26}}</ref> This ensures that every action is made by an authorized user, and that actions can be verified by anyone in possession of the public key used.
